page.title: Paths — Same age. Different starting lines.
page.description: Feel behind? Explore real lives, unequal starting points, work and randomness—without turning someone else’s outcome into a verdict on yours.

hero.eyebrow: For anyone who has ever felt behind
hero.title: same age. different *starting lines.*
hero.lede: Paths explores the work, advantages and accidents behind a life. The parts a comparison leaves out.
hero.note: An illustration of the essay’s metaphor

sections.title: the task is the same. *the starting line isn’t.*
sections.lede: A king and a peasant both water the flowers. Only one arrives with the jug already filled.

rows.title: the king
rows.body: Water found. Jug filled. Carried by others. Water the flowers.

rows.title: the peasant
rows.body: Find water → Fill the jug → Carry it. Water the flowers.

aside.title: the final action hides the work that made it possible.
aside.body: A metaphor, not a measured historical comparison.

sections.title: a breakthrough *has a backstory.*
sections.lede: Support and effort can coexist. So can preparation and an unexpected opening.

rows.title: age 13
rows.body: A school computer, years before most people had access.

rows.title: school years
rows.body: Manuals, peers and real programming work built experience.
Microsoft began after years of preparation.

rows.title: around age 3
rows.body: Family coaching began on Compton’s public courts.

rows.title: age 14
rows.body: Her first professional appearance ended in a qualifying loss.

rows.title: age 17
rows.body: Her first Grand Slam title followed years of practice.

rows.title: local stages
rows.body: She kept performing in South Wales pubs and clubs.
A scout heard her. An encounter opened a recording route.
A new collaboration brought Total Eclipse of the Heart.

sections.title: then the *world moves.*
sections.lede: A job. An investment. A move. A chance encounter. The same event can open one life and unsettle another.

rows.title: nvidia
rows.body: A job meets a wave.

rows.title: the housing crash
rows.body: A bargain. A loss.

rows.title: bangalore
rows.body: A frontier arrives nearby.

rows.title: the visa draw
rows.body: Qualified. Still waiting.

rows.title: bonnie tyler
rows.body: Someone was listening.

rows.title: the layoff
rows.body: A door closes.

rows.title: cursor
rows.body: A market starts moving.

rows.title: airbnb
rows.body: The company goes public.

rows.title: sandisk
rows.body: One company becomes two.

rows.title: the remote move
rows.body: Same salary. New city.

rows.title: shenzhen
rows.body: The map changes.

rows.title: the pizza coins

aside.title: work & making things · investing & ownership · place & moving · encounters & disruptions
aside.body: Dated examples, not investment advice or a forecast. Company valuations, share prices and money someone can spend are different things.

aside.title: about the evidence
aside.body: These are selected visible outcomes. Equally persistent people without the same result are missing.

sections.title: good attempts. *uncertain outcomes.*
sections.lede: A result tells you what happened. It cannot, by itself, tell you how good the decision was.

rows.title: a small experiment in randomness
rows.body: Two imaginary people. The same invented chance per attempt. A different number of attempts they can afford. Illustration only: a made-up one-in-six chance per attempt. Not your odds in life.

rows.title: who can afford to try again?
rows.body: Money, health, support and obligations are unequal too. More attempts are not a moral obligation. More attempts can create more chances. They do not promise an opening.

aside.title: what this experiment leaves out
aside.body: Real attempts differ: learning, connections, discrimination, costs and circumstances change them. An opening is not a final success. The experiment illustrates uncertainty; it cannot predict a person’s future.

aside.title: why a few big outcomes can distort the picture
aside.body: We see people after a breakthrough. We cannot count everyone who made similar attempts without one. That is survivorship bias, not evidence that the missing people tried less.

sections.title: give chance more *ways to find you.*
sections.lede: Not by doing everything. By making useful, affordable openings.

rows.title: put something real into the world.
rows.body: A small project, a useful contribution, a conversation beyond your usual circle. Work people can encounter creates occasions for feedback and connection.

rows.title: change the next attempt.
rows.body: Use feedback, deepen a skill, try a different audience. Repeating the same action is not always increasing your opportunities.

rows.title: keep the cost survivable.
rows.body: Time, health, money and responsibilities limit what is affordable. Smaller experiments, support, changing direction or pausing can preserve your choices.

aside.title: what supports this—and what doesn’t
aside.body: Experiments on LinkedIn found that weaker ties could improve job mobility, with effects varying by tie strength and industry. This supports a specific mechanism, not “more networking always wins.”

aside.title: first-person examples
aside.body: Pieter Levels and Marc Lou describe repeated launches and uneven returns. They are first-person examples, not proof that repeating their approach produces their results.

rows.title: who filled the king’s jug?
rows.body: The final action hides the work that made it possible.

rows.title: everyone has lost their marbles
rows.body: “Age is a timestamp, not a shared starting line.”

closing.title: you can want more. *you don’t have to be behind.*
closing.note: You didn’t choose every condition. You don’t have to earn the right to stop comparing. Keep your ambition, change it, or let some of it go. Meaningful work, security, relationships and a life you enjoy are not consolation prizes. No answer to submit. No score to improve.

footer.summary: An independent research exhibit about what people brought, what they were handed, what surrounded them, perseverance, luck, and the limits of comparison.
